evidence: src/application/order-service.ts, OrderService.addProduct: `if (!id.trim() || !name.trim() || !Number.isSafeInteger(stock) || stock < 0) throw new DomainError(...)`. This product invariant belongs in the domain layer, for example a createProduct function in src/domain/product.

src/application/order-service.ts, OrderService.placeOrder: `if (product.stock < item.quantity) throw new InsufficientStockError(...)` followed by `product.stock -= item.quantity`. The stock availability and reservation rule is applied in the application layer by mutating the domain entity directly.
src/application/order-service.ts, OrderService.cancelOrder: `product.stock += item.quantity` restores stock inline instead of through a domain operation.
Order rules are delegated to the domain via createOrder, transitionOrder and cancelOrder. This shows the intended split and that the product rules are misplaced.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService mostly orchestrates. It loads and saves through the FulfilmentStore port, delegates order rules to the domain (createOrder, transitionOrder, cancelOrder), and maps missing entities to NotFoundError. But it also carries Product business rules that belong in the domain layer. addProduct enforces the product invariants itself and throws a DomainError. placeOrder and cancelOrder apply the stock rule by mutating product.stock directly. Orders get domain functions for their rules, but products do not, so the product rules are misplaced in the application layer.

violations.message: Product business rules sit in the application layer, but they belong in the domain. addProduct validates the product invariants (non-empty id and name, non-negative integer stock) and throws DomainError. placeOrder and cancelOrder check and mutate product.stock inline (`product.stock < item.quantity`, `product.stock -= item.quantity`, `product.stock += item.quantity`). These should be domain functions on Product.
